## Solution

We determine the radius of convergence of
$$S(z) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} n^n z^{n^n}.$$

**Step 1: Rewrite as a standard power series.**

The series is a *lacunary* power series. Writing it as $\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} c_k z^k$, the coefficients are
$$c_k = \begin{cases} n^n & \text{if } k = n^n \text{ for some } n \ge 1, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}$$
(The single $n=0$ term is finite and does not affect the radius of convergence.)

**Step 2: Apply the Cauchy–Hadamard formula.**

The radius of convergence is
$$R = \frac{1}{\limsup_{k\to\infty} |c_k|^{1/k}}.$$

For indices $k = n^n$ (with $n \ge 1$),
$$|c_k|^{1/k} = (n^n)^{1/n^n} = n^{\,n/n^n} = n^{\,1/n^{n-1}}.$$
Taking logarithms,
$$\log\!\bigl(|c_k|^{1/k}\bigr) = \frac{\log n}{n^{n-1}} \xrightarrow{n\to\infty} 0,$$
since $n^{n-1}$ grows super-exponentially while $\log n$ grows slowly. Hence
$$|c_k|^{1/k} \to e^0 = 1 \quad \text{along the subsequence } k = n^n.$$

For all other indices $c_k = 0$, so $|c_k|^{1/k} = 0$. Therefore
$$\limsup_{k\to\infty} |c_k|^{1/k} = 1, \qquad R = \frac{1}{1} = 1.$$

**Step 3: Verify directly via the root test (sanity check).**

For a fixed $z$, the $n$-th term is $a_n = n^n z^{n^n}$. Its $n$-th root is
$$|a_n|^{1/n} = n\,|z|^{n^{n-1}}.$$

- If $|z| < 1$: $|z|^{n^{n-1}} \to 0$ super-exponentially, so $n|z|^{n^{n-1}} \to 0 < 1$. The series **converges**.
- If $|z| > 1$: $|z|^{n^{n-1}} \to \infty$, so $n|z|^{n^{n-1}} \to \infty > 1$. The series **diverges**.
- If $|z| = 1$: $|a_n| = n^n \to \infty$, so the terms do not tend to zero; the series **diverges**.

The series converges exactly on the open disk $|z| < 1$ and diverges on $|z| \ge 1$.

**Conclusion.** The radius of convergence is

$$\boxed{R = 1}.$$
